design_notes: Lead every paragraph with the plain point, then the filing's number, then the page tag. The financials section is where the temptation to data-dump is strongest — group the six periods into a pattern (loss to profit, a dip in FY2016, a negative cash-flow year in FY2017) before listing figures.

The single most interesting fact in this filing is that the company sells through its corporate promoter's network while being 99.76% promoter-owned. That is not a scandal and should not be written as one; explain what it means — the company rents distribution it does not own, and related-party transactions have already occurred in each of the last five years.

The offer section must be honest about what is missing. Say the excerpts do not disclose issue size, price band or the fresh-issue versus OFS split; do not soften this into 'details awaited' and do not construct a number.

There is no peer table and no price band, so no implied valuation range is computable. Do not write a valuation section and do not compare the company to unnamed 'industry peers'. Drop the section and let the governance and financials sections carry the analytical weight.
All figures arrive in ₹ lakh. Convert to ₹ crore throughout (divide by 100) and state the original unit once, early in the financials section, so the reader can follow the arithmetic.
Keep the risks section to exactly five company-specific risks. Competition belongs in the industry section where it is a market fact, not in the risk list where it would be boilerplate.

Watch the language around the promoter. 'Support of our holding company' is the filing's phrase for a strength; the same relationship is also listed as a risk factor. Report both without picking a verdict.
No recommendation, no verdict, no listing-gain language anywhere — including in headings and the standfirst.

kicker_candidates: From the DRHP, page by page

beats.beat: The company is a processor, not a miner or a formulator in the usual sense. It takes minerals and modifies them chemically, then sells the result into other people's products.
Four product families carry the revenue: Functional Additives and Chemically Modified Minerals on the specialty chemicals side, and Soft Minerals and Hard Minerals on the mineral side.

Distribution is borrowed, not built. The company markets and sells through the network of its Corporate Promoter, 20 Microns Limited, under a long-term arrangement — and the filing lists 'support of our holding company' as one of its stated strengths.
The customer list is short and the dependence is measurable: the top ten customers accounted for around 59% of revenue from operations in FY2017, 57% in FY2016 and 59% in FY2015.
Exports are a small, named slice: ₹1,068.18 lakh (about ₹10.68 crore) over the past five years, shipped to Nigeria, Saudi Arabia and Sri Lanka.

The filing's own list of strengths is the quickest summary of how it wants to be read: a diversified product portfolio, diversified user industries, import substitution, holding-company support, product innovation and R&D, and a management team.

The physical footprint is three plant sites and two offices: manufacturing at Plot 347 and Plot 9-10, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara, Gujarat, and at Plot 104/3, Thenkasi Road, Pathur Village, Alangulam, Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu, with administrative offices in Bhuj and Udaipur. The filing is explicit that the company does not own these premises.

business.heading: What the company actually does
business.purpose: Explain the product lines, how the products reach buyers, who the buyers are, and how concentrated that buyer list is.

beats.beat: The filing reports six periods, all restated: the six months ended 30 September 2017, and the financial years ended 31 March 2017, 2016, 2015, 2014 and 2013. The statements are in ₹ lakh; ₹100 lakh is ₹1 crore.

Profit after tax is small but has moved decisively. The company lost ₹0.27 crore in FY2013 and ₹0.12 crore in FY2014, then turned a profit of ₹1.50 crore in FY2015, ₹0.90 crore in FY2016, ₹1.75 crore in FY2017 and ₹1.33 crore in the six months to September 2017. The FY2016 dip between two stronger years is the thing to explain, not smooth over.

Per-share earnings track the same shape, assuming the share count is steady: basic earnings per share of negative ₹0.45 in FY2013, negative ₹0.20 in FY2014, ₹2.47 in FY2015, ₹1.46 in FY2016, ₹2.43 in FY2017 and ₹1.48 for the six months to September 2017.

Total assets have grown from ₹30.19 crore in FY2013 to ₹34.25 crore at 30 September 2017, but not in a straight line — they fell to ₹25.93 crore in FY2015 before climbing again through ₹27.67 crore in FY2016 and ₹32.74 crore in FY2017.

Operating cash flow is the least comfortable series in the filing: ₹2.01 crore in FY2013, ₹1.28 crore in FY2014, ₹4.22 crore in FY2015, ₹8.03 crore in FY2016, then negative ₹3.50 crore in FY2017, before a positive ₹1.25 crore in the six months to September 2017. A year of strong inflow followed by an outflow year is what the filing's own risk factor is pointing at.

Two disclosed balance-sheet items frame the downside. Contingent liabilities and commitments, to the extent not provided for, aggregated ₹29.11 lakh as at 30 September 2017. And the filing warns that unsecured loans taken by the company, the promoters, group companies or associates can be recalled by lenders at any time, while its loan agreements carry restrictive covenants.

Two things a reader would expect are not in the supplied pages: revenue from operations for any period, and the company's debt or EBITDA figures. Both should be flagged as not disclosed in the excerpts rather than approximated.

beats.beat: Four promoters are named: Mr. Chandresh S. Parikh, Mr. Atil C. Parikh, Mr. Rajesh C. Parikh and 20 Microns Limited, the corporate promoter whose sales network carries the company's products.

Pre-issue, the promoters hold 89,48,270 equity shares, or 99.76% of paid-up equity, and the promoter group excluding promoters holds a further 21,510 shares, or 0.24%. Outside shareholders hold effectively nothing before the issue.

The capital structure explains the share count. Authorised share capital was ₹2,000.00 lakh, being 20,00,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each; issued, subscribed and paid-up capital was ₹897.00 lakh, being 89,70,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, as at 30 September 2017.

The company has transacted with related parties in each of the last five financial years and in the six months to 30 September 2017, disclosed under Accounting Standard 18 in the financial statements. The filing's own risk factor says such transactions may continue and cannot be assured to be free of adverse effect.

Three compliance admissions sit close together in the risk section. There have been instances of non-filing, incorrect filing or delayed filing of statutory forms with the Registrar of Companies, later regularised with additional fees. Certain statutory and regulatory licences, registrations and approvals required to operate the manufacturing facility at Plot 9-10, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara have not been obtained, and the filing cannot assure the company will not be penalised. The corporate logo has not been registered.

The filing states that the company, its promoters, its group company and its directors are parties to legal proceedings, and that an adverse decision could have a material effect. It does not, in these excerpts, quantify those proceedings.

beats.beat: Specialty chemicals are the high-value, low-volume end of the chemicals business — sold for what they do to a customer's product rather than for their bulk. The filing prices that distinction: the Indian chemicals industry excluding pharmaceuticals and fertilisers was ₹5,800–6,200 billion in fiscal 2017, and specialty chemicals excluding agrochemicals and dyestuff were about 17% of it, at roughly ₹1,000 billion.
Growth is the pitch: specialty chemicals grew at 10–12% CAGR from fiscal 2014 to 2017, and CRISIL Research forecasts 12–14% CAGR going forward.

Growth is uneven inside the category, which matters for a small producer deciding where to push. Surfactants and water chemicals are projected at 13% and 15% CAGR over five years; construction chemicals and personal care ingredients at 15% over three years; textile chemicals and flavours and fragrances at 12%; polymer additives at 10% over three years.

The industry is not concentrated. It is highly fragmented, with small and medium enterprises holding 70–75% of the market, and the filing concedes that only a few Indian players have the scale or capability to compete with global giants on product development and innovation.

The demand drivers it lists are consumption and policy, not chemistry: rising intensity of consumption, an Indian middle class the filing says could reach 148 million households by 2030, a Draft National Chemical Policy aimed at lifting the chemicals share of GDP, permission for 100% foreign direct investment in the sector, and China's reduced focus on specialty chemicals after stricter environmental rules introduced in 2015.

The downstream customers are named and sized: paints at ₹401 billion in fiscal 2017, cosmetics and toiletries at ₹430–460 billion, polymer demand forecast at 9–10% CAGR between fiscals 2017 and 2020, and plastic products at 11–13% over the same window.

The headwinds are in the filing too. India's chemicals industry has imported more than it exported every year from 2012-13 to 2016-17, with imports growing at 6.4% CAGR against exports at 6%. Exports to Europe face the REACH registration regime, and GST replaced the earlier indirect-tax stack from 1 July 2017.
On the macro backdrop the filing anchors: India's GDP grew 7.1% in fiscal 2017, private consumption is 58% of GDP, and the urban share of the population was about 31% in 2011.

industry.heading: The market it sells into
industry.purpose: Give the reader a size and a growth rate for specialty chemicals in India, name the structure of the industry, and set out the headwinds the filing itself records.

beats.beat: 20 Microns Nano Minerals processes and sells specialty chemicals — functional additives and chemically modified minerals, plus soft minerals and hard minerals — and it is listing on the SME platform of the NSE.

One fact explains most of the company's shape: it does not have its own sales force for the network that carries its products. It has a long-term arrangement with its Corporate Promoter, 20 Microns Limited, to market and sell through the promoter's network.

The Parikh family and 20 Microns Limited own almost all of it — 99.76% of pre-issue equity sits with the promoters, and another 0.24% with the promoter group. A public listing is the first time outside shareholders get a stake.

What the money is for, in the filing's own list: capital expenditure on a new manufacturing facility at Plot 336, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara; general corporate purposes; and creating a public trading market on NSE Emerge.

The scale is small and the record is uneven: restated profit after tax ran from a ₹0.27 crore loss in FY2013 to ₹1.75 crore profit in FY2017, and operating cash flow was negative ₹3.50 crore in FY2017.

intro.purpose: Orient a reader who has never heard of this company: what it sells, who controls it, what it is raising money for, and how small the numbers are.

beats.beat: An Indian public issue can be a fresh issue, where the company creates and sells new shares and keeps the money, or an offer for sale, where existing owners sell their shares and the company gets nothing. Most SME issues are a mix.

The filing lists three objects. First, capital expenditure to set up a new manufacturing facility at Plot 336, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara, Gujarat. Second, general corporate purposes. Third, creating a public trading market for the shares by listing on the SME platform of NSE, NSE Emerge, which the filing says is to enhance visibility and brand.
Vivro Financial Services Private Limited is the lead manager to the issue.
Link Intime India Private Limited is the registrar.
The listing venue is NSE Emerge, the SME platform of the National Stock Exchange.

What the supplied excerpts do not disclose: the issue size, the price band, how the offer splits between a fresh issue and an offer for sale, whether any shareholder is selling, and the resulting post-issue shareholding. The reader should be told this is missing from the extracted pages rather than given a constructed figure.

offer.heading: The offer and what the money is for
offer.purpose: Explain the objects of the issue, name the lead manager and registrar, and state plainly which standard offer facts the supplied excerpts do not disclose.

beats.beat: Risk one: revenue rests on purchase orders, not contracts, and on very few buyers. The filing states there are no long-term or definitive agreements with customers and that sales terms are governed by purchase orders, while the top ten customers were 59%, 57% and 59% of revenue from operations in FY2017, FY2016 and FY2015. Lose two or three of those accounts and the top line moves.

Risk two: the company depends on a related party to sell its own products. Marketing and sales run through the network of the Corporate Promoter, 20 Microns Limited, under a long-term arrangement that the filing lists as a strength. The same filing warns that related-party transactions may continue and could adversely affect financial condition and results.

Risk three: regulatory gaps at an operating plant. The company has not obtained certain statutory and regulatory licences, registrations and approvals needed to operate the Plot 9-10, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara facility, and the filing says it cannot assure it will not be penalised. Separately, there have been non-filings, incorrect filings and delays with the Registrar of Companies, later regularised with additional fees.

Risk four: the cash flow turned negative and the borrowing is not fully secured. Operating cash flow was negative ₹3.50 crore in FY2017 against positive ₹8.03 crore in FY2016, and the filing carries its own risk factor on sustained negative cash flows. Unsecured loans taken by the company, the promoters, group companies or associates can be recalled at any time, and loan agreements carry restrictive covenants.

Risk five: the factories are not the company's. The company does not own the premises housing the manufacturing facilities at Plot 347, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara and at Plot 104/3, Thenkasi Road, Pathur Village, Alangulam, Tirunelveli, nor its administrative offices in Bhuj and Udaipur. Continuity of those leases is outside the company's control.

risks.heading: The five risks that matter most here
risks.purpose: Give five risks specific to this company, each with the filing's own words and the number that makes it concrete. No more than five.
